entries.title: ASEAN closing ranks as cyberscam threat escalates
entries.summary: Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Southeast Asian governments are searching for a joint strategy against cyberscammers, a criminal industry that has grown too big, too connected and too embedded in ASEAN economies to be solved just by policing.

For years, governments across Southeast Asia largely approached the region's online fraudsters as a matter for the police, anti-trafficking agencies and border authorities.

But these bodies have appearently failed to stem the rise of international cyberscam cartels. The illicit industry is increasingly using international banking systems, cryptocurrencies, telecommunications networks, shell companies and trafficking routes, with some of its centers operating under the protection of armed or politically connected groups.

Now, ASEAN governments seem increasingly willing to tackle the threat as a united bloc.

Myanmar approves death penalty for cyberscam bosses

Signs of this shift were visible at the controversial meeting in Bangkok on August 6 between Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Min Aung Hlaing, the head of Myanmar's military government.

The two governments agreed to clamp down on scam centres along their shared frontier, exchange information and jointly disrupt criminal financial flows.

Thailand also offered support for Myanmar's participation in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial-intelligence bodies. Myanmar's military-backed parliament had already voted in favour of applying the death penalty on those caught operating online scam centres.

While visiting Cambodia late last month, Indonesian Deputy Foreign Minister Arif Havas Oegroseno also proposed a joint task force to combat online scam syndicates.

And last week, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Thai Prime Minister Charnvirakul held talks in Jakarta where they agreed their two countries must lead the way and strengthen ASEAN's resilience against scam groups.

Online scams grew into an 'economic security threat'

A UN estimate published last month put the annual losses from cyber scammers — many of whom are located in Southeast Asia — at between $88.3 and $114.1 (between €76 billion and €98 billion) globally in 2025.

Artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies, encrypted communications and deepfake technology have made their operations cheaper and harder to detect.

"Cyber scams in Southeast Asia have evolved beyond a conventional cybercrime issue and should be viewed as an economic security threat," Hai Luong, a lecturer at Australia's Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice, told DW.

Impact of cybercrime felt around the world

Governments in Southeast Asia have already had to respond to pressure from the US, the EU and China as their online cartels drew international attention.

In October 2025, the US designated Cambodia's Prince Group, one of the country's largest conglomerates, as a transnational criminal organisation and imposed sanctions on 146 people and companies connected to it.

US authorities also charged Chinese-born Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies. Cambodia eventually revoked Chen's citizenship and extradited him to China.

Prince Group's business empire extended across real estate, finance and other sectors in Cambodia. US authorities allege that criminal revenues were mixed with legitimate commercial activities through an international network of companies.

Washington has also sanctioned other Southeast Asian individuals and companies accused of investing in scam compounds and laundering money.

The EU followed last month, imposing sanctions on Prince Group and Jin Bei Group in Cambodia and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army in Myanmar for alleged involvement in cyberscams.

Cambodia moves against US-sanctioned banks

In 2024, the United States Institute of Peace estimated that Cambodia's cyber-scam industry generated more than $12.5 billion annually, equivalent to roughly a third of the country's formal economy.

The collapse of several scam-linked conglomerates has raised concerns about how the economic shockwaves will affect the rest of the country. At the same time, other voices say negative publicity around scamming is hurting the country's tourism sector and keeping away foreign investors.

Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has acknowledged that the illicit scam economy is damaging legitimate businesses and has vowed a systematic crackdown on online scam networks, including greater scrutiny of the financial sector.

The National Bank of Cambodia has shuttered at least six financial institutions since the start of the year. Three commercial banks whose licences were revoked in August had all been sanctioned by the US over alleged links to scam networks.

On August 4, the Singaporean government introduced legislation that would expand information-sharing between police and service providers, allow authorities to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and strengthen restrictions on financial, telecommunications and online services supplied to suspected offenders.

Criminal groups capitalize on government inefficiencies

As ASEAN nations try to clamp down on cybercriminals, the region's greatest weakness is its fragmentation, Sophal Ear, an associate professor at Arizona State University's Thunderbird School of Global Management, told DW.

"Criminal organizations operate seamlessly across borders while governments continue responding through separate agencies with different mandates and limited coordination," he said.

Ear added that the financial infrastructure used to move and conceal criminal proceeds can often prove more resilient than the law-enforcement architecture designed to dismantle it.

What is in ASEAN's anti-crime plan?

Now, the regional governments seem to be catching on — at least judging by ASEAN's new Plan of Action in Combating Transnational Crime for 2026–2035.

The plan calls for improved intelligence-sharing between national law-enforcement agencies and financial-intelligence units, joint investigations, better cross-border coordination and stronger capacity among anti-money-laundering regulators.

ASEAN has also recently established a joint working group to combat money laundering.

But ASEAN's consensus-based system still heavily relies on national governments implementing those commitments and sharing sensitive financial and law-enforcement information.

"In practice, governments should prioritise disrupting the financial infrastructure, labour supply chains, technological services, and transnational business models that sustain scam operations rather than focusing solely on individual offenders," said Luong from Griffith University's School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Moving beyond money mules

Asha Hemrajani, senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, agreed that the region needs to take a "holistic, not siloed" approach to attack the entire cyberscam business model.

"The shared objective should be to identify and dismantle crime syndicate leadership, financial networks and enabling infrastructure, not just arrest money mules or raid individual scam compounds in Cambodia and Myanmar," Hemrajani said.

This includes official scrutiny of high-risk corporate structures and checking sources of funding, as well as a much tougher stance against money laundering, she added. Hemrajani also recommended ASEAN sanctioning business groups linked to the cyberscam networks, similar to how Washington cut off sanctioned Southeast Asian companies from the entire US economy.

Criminal groups have largely survived previous crackdowns by simply moving workers, technology and money to new places and new compounds. In order to fight the online cartels, ASEAN should do more than just closing scam centres. The real challenge is making the regional economy itself harder for them to exploit.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: India: Student anger over alleged exam issues spreads to Jharkhand
entries.summary: Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.
entries.content:
India

India: Anger over exam irregularities spreads to Jharkhand

August 10, 2026

Inspired by the Cockroach movement, young people in India's eastern state of Jharkhand are marching on the state assembly to demand transparency and a probe into alleged irregularities in civil service recruitment exams.

Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process.

Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly.

The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters.

The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi.

In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led "Cockroach" protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike.

Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated.

"The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW.

He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned.

But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs.

What sparked the protests in Jharkhand?

The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July.

Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated.

Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure.

But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem.

What are the protesters' demands?

The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated.

They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery.

The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies.

The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken.

"The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW.

Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India?

The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers.

That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan .

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters.

But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined.

Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi.

"Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system," Bora told DW. 

"They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future."

Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights.

Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition.

"Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW.

"The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added.

Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12.

"The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment.

Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government

The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media, hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. 

The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission.

But India's youth are refusing to stop there.

Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure.  

For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest.

"We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino
entries.summary: A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.
entries.content:
Europe

UEFA, other football federations unite against Infantino

August 10, 2026

A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured football executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.

Gianni Infantino's already perilous position as FIFA president took another blow on Monday, as three continental football federations banded together in an apparent attempt to try to force him out.

An "Open Letter to the Football Family" signed by the heads of UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia) appeared to take aim at Infantino —  without actually mentioning him by name.

"This is about something more fundamental: the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it. Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding — or demanding — power to be held," the statement read.

"It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

The letter criticizes Infantino's now scrapped plan to form a subsidiary arm of FIFA (International Federation of Association Football) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors.

It says that even in withdrawing the plan, FIFA "did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong."

It also labels the plan a "fundamental breach of trust" and lambasted Infantino's seemingly unilateral actions in bypassing the executive FIFA Council for his initial proposal and then holding a summit in Morocco with only selected senior figures within the organization.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness," the letter reads.

The statement comes after media reports that UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Infantino during his time at the European confederation. FIFA in response criticized "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims" and said that "it is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President."

FIFA have not yet replied to a DW request for comment on the open letter.

What does this change for Infantino?

Were the national federations of the three confederations to fall in line, there would be easily enough votes to oust Infantino at the presidential election in March 2027. FIFA has 211 voting members and thus a presidential candidate in a two-horse race would require 106 votes. UEFA (55 members) AFC (46) and CONCACAF (35) would easily have enough if each confederation's members voted as a bloc.

However, this seems unlikely. While UEFA, who have driven much of the opposition, seem relatively united, the picture in the two other confederations is more mixed. Mexico, one of CONCACAF's most powerful nations and a World Cup 2026 cohost, have backed Infantino while Qatar, who hosted the 2022 World Cup, is one of several Asian nations to have broken ranks.

The South American federation CONMEBOL (10) does not yet have a clear position on Infantino, but one of its most powerful nations, Argentina, have lent Infantino their support. The Oceania federation (11) has also yet to make its position clear.

Perhaps the best news for Infantino was the backing of the African confederation, CAF (54), last week.

A statement from the organization's executive committee said that CAF "unanimously reconfirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino and thanked him for his support for African Football over the years."

Is there a candidate to challenge Infantino?

This is the big question. As it stands, no candidate has stepped forward. Infantino won the last presidential election unopposed and looked likely to do so again next March, until a few weeks ago.

Though the clear positioning of several confederations against Infantino suggests that running unopposed again is now unlikely, a candidate that can unite those federations in opposition to the Swiss administrator is the next step.

"There's such an imperative to get a candidate who could unite the whole world of football, not just Europe in this case," UEFA vice president, Laura McAllister, recently told DW.

"It's not as easy as people might think. The right candidate has to also have the right level of support," McAllister said. "But if we're talking about the right candidate, then I think that person, that man or woman, needs to be somebody who recognizes that we are simply custodians of the sport and that we look after it and hopefully leave it in better health."

What might happen next?

There will no doubt be plenty of backroom talks about finding a candidate and announcing them at the right time. But given that Infantino retains a reasonable amount of support, football's powerbrokers will likely want to ensure whoever they might put up can win. UEFA executives will likely discuss this at the Super Cup (between the winners of last season's Champions League and Europa League) later this week, while other federations will look to do similar.

Looming in early September is the first FIFA tournament since the controversial sell-off plan was announced. The U-20 Women's World Cup is being held in Poland, a UEFA member, and it is not yet clear whether European teams will participate in the tournament with Infantino still in charge.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia
entries.summary: Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia

August 10, 2026

Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least 13 people and wounded 48 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

Ukraine's military ⁠said ⁠it struck the Taneco oil refinery overnight, adding that a ⁠fire was recorded at the site.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Thai ex-lawmaker shoots local official dead over loan
entries.summary: A former lawmaker confessed to shooting a senior official at a government office over a money dispute, police have said. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

A former lawmaker confessed to shooting a senior official at a government office over a money dispute, police have said. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.

Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok.

Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting.

Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money.

"I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired."

Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital.

Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said no one in Thailand other than on-duty officials was allowed to carry a gun in public. He pointed out that the last gun-carry licences were issued three years ago and were only valid for one year.

He said authorities will pursue "full legal action" against Chalong, a former member of the prime minister's party.

"No matter who he is, he is now a murderer," Anutin said.

Police: Shooting a 'personal issue'

Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue."

"According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300).

Second recent shooting

This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Prime Minister Anutin had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns.

Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: India news: Jharkhand police use tear gas, water cannons to disperse student protesters
entries.summary: Police used force to disperse students marching towards the Jharkhand assembly, as protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams entered their third week. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Jharkhand police use tear gas on student protesters

Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026

Police used force to disperse students marching towards the Jharkhand assembly, as protests over alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams entered their third week. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi
  • TG Mohandas was arrested in Kerala over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the student protests last month
  • Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the Cockroach Janta Party-led movement are facing severe online harassment
  • Model Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest
  • Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, August 10:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Assam flood toll climbs to 100

Assam flood toll climbs to 100

The situation in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll in the floods reaching 100, officials said.

Two more people died overnight on Sunday after weeks of heavy monsoon rain inundated villages, damaged roads and farmland and disrupted livelihoods.

More than 700,000 people have been displaced since the floods began last month, while about 49,000 remain in 125 relief camps and distribution centers, officials said.

Authorities are warning that, several rivers, including the Brahmaputra, remained above danger levels, raising the risk of further flooding in vulnerable areas.

Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, that in a nearby village of 100 houses only a few remain.

"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle," he said, according to the Associated Press.

Authorities are assessing the damage and providing financial assistance to affected residents. According to the government about 50,000 people had already received interim compensation.

While flooding is a recurring problem in Assam during the monsoon, experts warn that climate change is making rainfall increasingly erratic and extreme.

Skip next section Jharkhand student protests: Police use water cannons to disperse marching students

Jharkhand student protests: Police use water cannons to disperse marching students

Police used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi in the eastern state of Jharkhand on Monday, reports said. 

On Sunday, the sixth round of talks between student protesters and the government failed to reach a breakthrough after students alleged irregularities in government recruitment exams.

The sit-in protests in Jharkhand began on July 25.

Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 2 is demanding action over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC), Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission Combined Graduate Level (JSSC CGL) and other competitive examinations required to qualify for government jobs.

Meanwhile, authorities on Monday arrested former Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) chairperson L Khiangte in connection with alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations, reports said.

Earlier, Chief Minister Hemant Soren has assured the protesting students that his government would take action over alleged exam irregularities and invited them for talks.

Skip next section Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

Court calls sexual harassment allegations against former wrestling chief 'fabricated'

A Delhi court called the sexual harassment allegations against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh "false and fabricated" and part of a "deep conspiracy which seems to be politically motivated," media reports said.

Singh was acquitted last week of the sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by female athletes. The former lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had denied allegations that he groped wrestlers and demanded sexual favors.

In its detailed judgment, the court cited "material contradictions" in the wrestlers’ accounts, inconsistencies between their allegations and documentary evidence, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints, media reports said.

The court said some allegations appeared "rehearsed, well-practiced and planted."

Lawyer Rebecca John, who represented four of the women, described the acquittal as "deeply, deeply disturbing" on Monday, news channel NDTV reported.

The allegations had triggered months of protests in New Delhi in 2023, led by prominent Indian wrestlers with hundreds joining the sit-in demonstrations accusing authorities of failing to act against Singh.

Delhi police charged Singh in 2023, and a court formally brought charges against him in 2024 over allegations involving five women.

Skip next section Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest

Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest

Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who gained attention after standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month's Cockroach Janta Party-led demonstrations, has spoken about facing online abuse and threats following the protest.

In an interview with DW's Shalu Yadav, Ahir said the attention had come at a "heavy price" of online trolling and harassment, adding that women should be able to express their views without being targeted.

She referred to comments made about women protesters, including comments that they "should be raped" and would "enjoy it," saying such remarks could influence others and should not be allowed to go unchallenged.

"I read one comment saying 'we are going to rip you apart from the middle. And nobody's going to come to lay flowers on your grave,'" she said.

Ahir described the attacks as "criminal."

"I will not let it slide," she said. "I will not let them feel that they can sit behind their blank screens and feel so powerful by belittling other people.

Her comments come amid a wider online campaign targeting women who took part in the CJP-led protests, with reports of fake and AI-manipulated images, doxxing and threats against participants.

Skip next section Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters

Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters

An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said.

The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest.

According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped."

He also called for police to open fire at protesters.

News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator.

The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said.

Women protesters being targeted online

The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment. They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats.

Additionally, their phone numbers and home addresses have been leaked online alongside targeted attacks against their family members.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

Female protesters who took part in Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstrations against the government are facing harassment and doxxing. In the latest development, a right-wing activist was arrested in the southern state of Kerala for allegedly posting a video saying that those attending the protests "like rape."

Meanwhile, a Delhi court has said allegations of sexual harassment made by women wrestlers against former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh were "false" and "fabricated."

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

entries.title: When extreme heat threatens Europe's nuclear power
entries.summary: Warm rivers and low water levels are forcing nuclear power plants to reduce output across Europe. Over a year, the losses are minimal, but on critical days the loss of power has consequences for grids and prices.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Warm rivers and low water levels are forcing nuclear power plants to reduce output across Europe. Over a year, the losses are minimal, but on critical days the loss of power has consequences for grids and prices.

The state of the Danube is currently showing just how dependent nuclear power plants are on their local conditions. At the power station in Paks, Hungary — which normally produces about 40% of the country's electricity needs — only one of four turbine units is still operating. Due to record-low water levels in the Danube, the country's only nuclear power plant was even briefly at risk of a complete shutdown.

But for the European electricity market, France is of far greater significance. No other country in Europe relies so heavily on nuclear power, and if output in France drops, the country supplies less electricity to its neighbors, and may even become an electricity importer itself.

Reduced power

Over the course of the entire year, heat-related production losses at French power plants are minimal, but during individual weeks of extreme heat, the restrictions can be significant.

A 2023 report by France's official audit office estimated that, between 2000 and 2022, annual losses across all of the country's nuclear reactors due to high water temperatures and low river levels amounted to less than 1% of annual nuclear power production in any given year. Even in the extremely hot summer of 2003, they amounted to only about 1.5%.

But the annual figures obscure short-term fluctuations. In the summer of 2003, French nuclear power plants had to temporarily reduce their output by more than six gigawatts, and the most recent heat waves at the end of June and in mid-July 2026 saw the maximum available capacity was temporarily limited by eight to nine gigawatts. This corresponds to up to one-fifth of the nuclear power capacity normally available to France in the summer.

But eight gigawatts less capacity is not the same as an eight gigawatt overall shortfall. Even without the low water levels, some reactors would not be running at full capacity — either because of lower summer demand, high solar-power production, or bottlenecks in the power grid. According to grid operators, France still had sufficient reserves even during the 2026 heat waves and, on balance, remained an electricity exporter.

Other countries feel the impact

Nevertheless, such restrictions are relevant for grid operators and electricity traders. For them, it doesn't matter how much electricity was ultimately produced by nuclear power plants at the end of the year: What is crucial for the stability of the power grids and short-term price surges is whether the power is actually available when it is needed.

And here, experience shows that heat waves increase electricity demand due to air conditioning. Not only that: As this year's heat waves are affecting large parts of Europe, reserves from abroad are also declining.

Rivers getting warmer

Nuclear power plants suffer from low water levels because they must discharge a comparatively large amount of waste heat per kilowatt-hour generated. Only about one-third of the heat generated in a nuclear reactor is converted into electricity; the rest is released into the environment via the cooling system — often into rivers or the sea. But if the river is carrying little water, the waste heat is distributed over a smaller volume of water, and the water temperature rises faster.

Warm water also contains less oxygen, and legal temperature limits are in place to protect fish and other aquatic life. When operators throttle back a reactor in the summer, it is therefore usually not an emergency shutdown for reactor safety, but rather a measure to protect the local river life.

In critical situations, French authorities occasionally grant exemptions from these limits. In such cases, water bodies are monitored more closely, allowing the state-owned power company EdF to produce additional electricity in the short term.

A power plant with cooling towers draws significantly less water from the river and discharges considerably less heat directly into the water than a plant with an open cooling circuit. However, cooling towers do not make a nuclear power plant independent of weather conditions, as the Golfech plant demonstrates.

Located on the Garonne River, which is particularly warm in summer and frequently experiences low water levels, it is one of the most vulnerable sites, despite its cooling towers.

Meanwhile in Chooz on the Meuse River, the reactors had to be throttled back in 2020 despite the cooling towers, to avoid jeopardizing the drinking water supply in Belgium.

Repairs also reduce output

Not every decline in nuclear power production can be explained by the weather. Four years ago, France's reactors generated nearly 82 terawatt-hours less electricity than in 2021. This headline-grabbing crisis was caused less by climate change than by stress corrosion cracking and postponed maintenance work.

But looking ahead, the French audit office expects that climate-related reactor downtime could triple or even quadruple by 2050. Given the low baseline so far, even that would not yet constitute a widespread outage, but it could become critical for individual sites.

With additional cooling towers, deeper water intake structures, and better maintenance planning, France can at least partially counteract this trend. However, making the power plants more heat-resistant costs a lot of money and requires more land.

In its upcoming nuclear power plant modernization program, France intends to take the consequences of climate change into account. Four of the six modern EPR2 reactors initially planned are to be built on the coast, in Penly and Gravelines. Only the third pair of reactors will be built on the Rhone River near Bugey. Cooling towers there are intended to limit the thermal load on the river and water intake.

Consequences across Europe

The consequences of French reactor curtailments are evident in the European electricity market. On June 24, capacity was reduced by approximately 4.1 gigawatts due to high river temperatures. As a result, France's electricity exports fell to about three gigawatts, after the country had supplied 10 to 12 gigawatts to its neighbors just the week before.

Combined with higher electricity consumption, low wind power generation, and increased use of gas-fired power plants, this contributed to electricity prices in France and Germany briefly climbing to their highest levels since January 2025.

During the subsequent heat waves in July, the curtailment of reactors was even more extensive, though the impact on other countries was less significant. On July 13, eight reactors with a combined capacity of 6.3 gigawatts were affected, and two were completely taken offline. Nevertheless, France only intermittently exported more than 10 gigawatts and imported affordable solar and wind power from Spain.

The heat-related curtailments of nuclear power plants currently appear to be a manageable problem for the country. Whether this will develop into a Europe-wide shortage in the future will likely depend not least on the development of foreign demand and the reserves of wind and solar power.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: China: Typhoon Dolphin prompts mass evacuation, canceled flights
entries.summary: Even as it weakens, Typhoon Dolphin is disrupting life in China. Close to 1,500 flights have been canceled in Shanghai while parts of Beijing are under flood alert.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

Even as it weakens, Typhoon Dolphin is disrupting life in China. Close to 1,500 flights have been canceled in Shanghai while parts of Beijing are under flood alert.

Heavy rainfall and strong winds prompted flood alerts and more than 1,000 flight cancellations across China on Monday, even as Typhoon Dolphin weakened.

China's National Meteorological Centre (NMC) issued its least severe typhoon alert on Monday morning as the storm lost power after making landfall in China's Zhejiang Province on Sunday.

Despite the weaker storm, the NMC warned that parts of east and central China will continue to receive heavy rainfall. Authorities issued their most severe flash flood alert for parts of eastern and southern Zhejiang on Monday, state news broadcaster CCTV reported.

Five districts in Beijing are also under red alerts for heavy rainfall on Monday, with risks of landslides and flooding.

The storm had already forced over 300,000 people in eastern China to preemptively relocate, while bringing heavy rainfall to northern Taiwan over the weekend. In Shanghai, authorities evacuated more than 30,000 people out of high-risk areas. Overall, some one million people have been told to seek shelter.

Typhoon Dolphin disrupts transport in Shanghai

Shanghai's two main passenger airports, Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, canceled 943 flights between them for Monday, the airport authority said in a post online. That's a reduction of capacity by nearly 40%.

On Sunday, the two airports had cancelled nearly 1,500 flights, or about 60% of their scheduled travel, according to state media.

Public transport services in the city were also impacted, with several local trains suspended.

At the same time, Zhejiang province began to resume its transport facilities.

Zhejiang's Ningbo International Airport will resume flights midday on Monday but warned that some of the scheduled travel may still be delayed or canceled as the storm had "not yet completely dissipated."

China is dealing with Typhoon Dolphin just two weeks after Typhoon Noul struck its southern Guangdong province. Last month, Typhoon Maysak killed 11 people and injured over 300 in the central Hubei province.

Extreme weather systems are a common feature in China this time of the year, with typhoons leaving significant displacement, infrastructural damage and loss of lives. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of such extreme weather have increased and will continue to rise amid climate change.  

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Germany news: Low water on Rhine could sever freight route
entries.summary: Germany's inland shipping association has warned that the Rhine could soon become effectively split in two as water levels continue to fall. In Berlin, a man was shot dead near a busy central transport hub. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Low water on Rhine could sever freight route

Published August 10, 2026last updated August 10, 2026

Germany's inland shipping association has warned that the Rhine could soon become effectively split in two as water levels continue to fall. In Berlin, a man was shot dead near a busy central transport hub. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Commercial shipping along the full length of the Rhine River could soon become impossible
  • Historic low-water levels were recorded at several points on the river over the weekend
  • A man was shot dead near Berlin's Zoo station after a dispute involving several people

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, August 10, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Kane to receive European Golden Shoe in Munich

Kane to receive European Golden Shoe in Munich

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is set to receive the European Golden Shoe on August 19 after finishing as the continent's leading league scorer last season.

Both the Bundesliga and Bayern say the England captain is to be presented with the European Sports Media award at an event in the FC Bayern Museum.

Kane scored 36 Bundesliga goals last season, finishing well ahead of Manchester City's Erling Haaland and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe in their respective leagues.

The 33-year-old will receive the trophy for the second time, having also scored 36 goals in his first season with Bayern in 2023/24.

The Golden Shoe has been awarded to Europe's top league goalscorer since 1968.

Former Bayern forwards Gerd Müller, in 1970 and 1972, and Robert Lewandowski, in 2021 and 2022, also won the award twice.

Skip next section Germany sees Trump's Gaza plan as chance for progress

Germany sees Trump's Gaza plan as chance for progress

The German government has described US President Donald Trump's latest Gaza plan as an opportunity to make progress toward disarming Hamas.

A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Monday that some disagreement over the proposal was to be expected after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the plan.

"With such a complex undertaking, it was perfectly clear there would be many, many unanswered questions," the spokesperson was quoted by Reuters news agency as saying.

Skip next section Economist urges Germany to rethink defense spending

Economist urges Germany to rethink defense spending

Germany risks pouring hundreds of billions of euros into outdated military technology instead of preparing for future warfare, the head of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW) has warned.

IfW President Moritz Schularick criticized Defense Minister Boris Pistorius for continuing to spend heavily on tanks, frigates and other conventional systems rather than prioritizing artificial intelligence, robotics, drones and satellite technology.

"We have a lot of capital, a lot of industrial know-how and, in some areas, still highly advanced technologies," Schularick told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

"What we don't have are hundreds of thousands of people who want to get into tanks and go to the front," he said.

Germany should therefore rely wherever possible on AI, robotics, drones and satellites rather than simply increasing troop numbers, manned vehicles and barracks, he argued.

Schularick said Germany's roughly €700 billion ($809 billion) program to modernize and strengthen the Bundeswehr risked failing to deliver unless procurement was fundamentally overhauled.

Skip next section German rents keep rising amid housing shortage

German rents keep rising amid housing shortage

Rents for new leases in Germany have continued to rise sharply as a persistent housing shortage keeps pressure on the market, a survey shows.

New rents for apartments in multi-family buildings were 3.2% higher in the second quarter than a year earlier, according to the Association of German Pfandbrief Banks (VDP).

The pace of growth eased somewhat compared with previous quarters, however.

Across Germany’s seven largest cities, rents rose by an average of just 1.5%, but the picture varied sharply.

Düsseldorf recorded the strongest increase at 3.6%, while rents in Berlin were almost unchanged, rising just 0.6%.

Germany is estimated to be short of around 1 million homes, with supply particularly tight in major urban areas.

Home prices also continued to climb in the second quarter.

Apartments and houses were 1.9% more expensive than a year earlier and 0.3% higher than in the previous quarter, the VDP said.

Prices in the seven biggest cities rose 2.1% year-on-year, led by Hamburg at 3.8%.

Cologne followed with 2.5%, while Frankfurt and Düsseldorf both recorded increases of 2.4%.

Skip next section German nurse murder probe expands to over 120 cases

German nurse murder probe expands to over 120 cases

German prosecutors are investigating scores more suspected cases involving a former nurse already convicted of murdering 10 patients.

Prosecutors in the western German city of Aachen say the probe extends to more than 120 additional cases.

They said 39 bodies had so far been exhumed as part of the widening investigation. Authorities in Cologne, who are conducting a separate probe, have exhumed another seven bodies.

The former nurse was sentenced to life imprisonment by Aachen Regional Court last November for 10 murders and 27 attempted murders. The court also found a particular severity of guilt, making release after 15 years unlikely.

According to the verdict, the man administered excessive doses of sedatives to seriously ill patients during night shifts at a hospital in the town of Würselen, sometimes combining them with painkillers or administering repeated doses.

The alleged motives were the man's own sense of personal unease and desire for order.

The nurse denied the allegations during his trial.

The offenses covered by his conviction took place between December 2023 and May 2024. The new investigation concerns possible killings before that period.

Skip next section Germany's hot summer part of record western Europe heat

Germany's hot summer part of record western Europe heat

Germany has been hit by repeated heatwaves, worsening drought and exceptionally low river levels this summer.

New Copernicus data shows the bigger picture: western Europe has just recorded its hottest June and July on record.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Share of young people in Germany remains at record low

Share of young people in Germany remains at record low

Young people continue to make up a historically small share of Germany's population, according to figures from the Federal Statistical Office.

At the end of 2025, around 8.3 million people were aged between 15 and 24, representing 10% of the population.

That share has remained at a record low since the beginning of the 2020s.

The proportion of young people was highest in the first half of the 1980s, when the baby boomer generation was still in this age group.

In 1983, around one in six people in what is now Germany, or 16.7%, were aged 15 to 24.

Young people make up a larger share of the population among people with an immigration background.

The share of young people also varies by region.

Bremen had the highest proportion at 11.1%, followed by Hamburg at 10.5% and Baden-Württemberg at 10.4%. Brandenburg had the lowest share at 8.8%, while Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Saxony-Anhalt each stood at 9.1%.

Germany also remained slightly below the European Union average. Young people accounted for 10% of the population, compared with an EU average of 10.7%.

Skip next section Minimum wage violations cost Germany billions, union says

Minimum wage violations cost Germany billions, union says

Illegal practices used to evade Germany's minimum wage have cost workers, social security funds and the state as much as €64 billion over a decade, according to calculations by the German Trade Union Confederation (DGB).

The DGB estimates that an average of around two million workers a year have received less than the legal minimum since it was introduced in 2015.

The shortfall amounted to roughly €1.70 to €2.40 per hour, based on survey data on working hours and earnings.

For the period from 2015 to 2024, the union calculated that workers missed out on around €35 billion in pay.

A further €22 billion was lost to social security funds and about €7 billion in income tax revenue.

Germany's main employers' association said minimum wage violations were unacceptable and should be investigated and prosecuted, but urged caution over the DGB figures.

It said survey data could be imprecise, particularly when working hours were not recorded accurately.

Germany's statutory minimum wage currently stands at €13.90 an hour and applies to around six million workers, especially in sectors such as hospitality, retail and agriculture.

Skip next section Germany to speed up drone defenses at airports

Germany to speed up drone defenses at airports

Germany has promised to accelerate upgrades to drone detection and defense systems at its airports following last week's explosive-drone incident at Leipzig/Halle.

"Reliable detection is absolutely crucial," Transport Minister Steffen Bilger told the news website Politico on Monday.

Bilger said Germany's air navigation service provider is responsible for safety in the airspace around airports and that early detection therefore plays a key role.

He said Frankfurt and Munich are already better equipped, but warned that other airports need to catch up quickly.

"We have no time to lose," Bilger said. "I want to accelerate further upgrades wherever possible."

The push follows the discovery last week of a drone carrying an explosive device in a secure cargo area at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

A federal police bomb disposal team defused the device.

Several Ukrainian cargo aircraft were nearby at the time. The airport is used as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine.

Skip next section Man shot dead near Berlin's Zoo station

Man shot dead near Berlin's Zoo station

A 30-year-old man has been shot dead following a dispute involving several people near Berlin's busy Zoologischer Garten station.

Paramedics tried to resuscitate the victim, but he died at the scene, police said.

The suspected attackers fled and remain at large.

Police did not say how many shots were fired shortly before midnight, and the circumstances surrounding the dispute remain unclear.

A homicide unit has taken over the investigation.

The shooting took place at one of western Berlin's busiest transport hubs, close to the Kurfürstendamm shopping boulevard and the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church.

The case comes amid a marked rise in firearms incidents in the German capital.

Berlin police recorded 1,119 cases involving firearms in 2025, up 68% from 2024. Shots were actually fired in more than 500 of those cases.

Police chief Barbara Slowik Meisel said earlier this year that disputes once settled with fists were now increasingly involving guns.

Other recent cases include shots fired at a restaurant window in Neukölln early on Sunday and the shooting of a 38-year-old man in the city's Schöneberg district the previous weekend.

Skip next section Rhine could become impassable at key shipping point

Rhine could become impassable at key shipping point

The Rhine River could soon become effectively split in two for commercial shipping as water levels continue to fall amid persistent dry weather, Germany's inland shipping association has warned.

Jens Schwanen, managing director of the Federal Association of German Inland Navigation, said the gauge at Kaub, a crucial point for freight traffic, was forecast to fall into single digits for the first time this week.

"Commercial shipping will no longer be able to transport goods in the region at such low water levels," Schwanen told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

He said excursion boats and river cruises would also be affected.

"In principle, the Rhine would then no longer be continuously navigable and would be divided into two," Schwanen said.

Shipping would still be possible between the ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Antwerp and parts of North Rhine-Westphalia, roughly as far as Cologne.

Further south, traffic could continue on tributaries and connected waterways including the Neckar, Moselle, Main and Main-Danube Canal.

Historic low-water levels were recorded at several points on the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia over the weekend after weeks of dry weather and too little rainfall across the river's catchment area.

The falling river is already forcing freight vessels to carry much lighter loads, pushing up transport costs for industries that depend on bulk cargo.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn on the banks of the Rhine.

An inland shipping group is warning that, very soon, the river — Europe's most important inland commercial waterway — could no longer be navigable along its full length.

Germany's inland shipping association warned that the gauge at a crucial point for freight traffic could drop into single digits this week.

At such low levels, commercial vessels would no longer be able to transport goods through that stretch of the river.

Meanwhile, police are investigating a fatal shooting in a busy part of Berlin after a dispute involving several people.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of the things that Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Type 2 diabetes in young women increasingly common
entries.summary: British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most among women under 40. The disease is often underdiagnosed in women or diagnosed too late to reverse the condition's progression.
entries.content:
August 10, 2026

British researchers say rates of type 2 diabetes are growing most among women under 40. The disease is often underdiagnosed in women or diagnosed too late to reverse the condition's progression.

There used to be a clear-cut way to distinguish diabetes type 1 and type 2. Medical jargon aside: Type 1 diabetes was a genetic autoimmune disease that presented in young people, and type 2 was a disease that presented in older patients in their fifties or sixties due to an unhealthy lifestyle. 

But that distinction of young and old doesn't work anymore.

More and more, younger people are being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. In England, for example, the biggest increase in new diagnoses of type 2 diabetes is among young women.

This was revealed when a team of researchers from Imperial College London evaluated data from an English National Diabetes Audit between 2011 and 2024. They found that while the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was decreasing in adults between 60 and 79 years of age, it was rising in under-40-year-olds.

The results, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe journal, showed the sharpest increase was among white, Asian and Black women in their 20s, and white women in their 30s.

"Much of the discussion around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people has focused on ethnic minority groups," said Shivani Misra, the lead author of the study and a clinical associate professor for diabetes at Imperial College London.

"While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected with early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is […] increasing in white populations too, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation."

Lifestyle behind rise in type 2 diabetes among young people

In Germany, the situation is similar to the UK, said Baptist Gallwitz, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for the German Diabetes Society (DDG).

"Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in many countries," Gallwitz told DW. "It's basically a pandemic. In Germany, we're also seeing an increase in children and teenagers diagnosed with the disease."

From 2014 to 2023, there was an increase in type 2 diabetes cases of 5.8% a year among youth aged 11 to 17 years, according to a 2026 health report on diabetes released by the DDG.  

While genetic disposition can play a role in the development of type 2 diabetes, the biggest factor is lifestyle.

"We live in a world where we don't move enough and where our nutrition contains too much sugar and too many calories," Gallwitz said. "That leads to more obesity among young people, and that in turn greatly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes."

In people with type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin secretion or a weaker effect of insulin on its receptors lead to a higher glucose content in the blood.

Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a full loss of insulin-producing cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency.

Fighting the rise of diabetes type 2 in young people

The increase is particularly concerning because in young patients, the progression of the disease can be more serious than in older patients.

"Any diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is serious, but it can be more aggressive in younger people, increasing the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short," said Helen Kirrane from Diabetes UK, a charity that campaigns on the issue.

That's why it's important to intervene early. Gallwitz said the DDG welcomed the introduction of a tax on sugary sodas in Germany, but added that it wasn't enough.

The DDG is calling for a tiered value-added tax (VAT) system, with fresh fruit and vegetables being sold with no tax and the VAT increasing the more the products contain saturated fats and sugars.

The organization also wants healthier food in kindergarten and school cafeterias and one hour of mandatory movement per day to be incorporated into class schedules.

Asking for more exercise during the school day is one thing. But conditions in the general environment also need to be improved to stop the increase of type 2 diabetes in young women, said Alexandra Kautzky-Willer, head of the division for endocrinology and metabolism at the Medical University of Vienna.

"More movement is important, so we need to ensure conditions in which it's safe for women to move," Kautzky-Willer, who is also a professor of gender medicine, told DW.

For example, a woman who fears being catcalled, ridiculed for her weight or even attacked in the dark is less likely to go running after work or join a gym.

Diabetes type 2 underdiagnosed in women

The number of women with type 2 diabetes might be even higher than what current data show. In 2025, Kautzky-Willer and a colleague wrote a report for the Deutsches Ärzteblatt, a German medical journal, saying that the disease is underdiagnosed in women.

"Men are usually diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes] at a younger age," they wrote in the the article. "At the point of diagnosis, more women are obese, they have hypertension more often and have gained more weight" than men when they are diagnosed.

Those factors contributed to an increased risk of stroke and heart attacks as well. So, why is it that diabetes type 2 is often only diagnosed in women when they are already this sick?

"For one, the value often tested in initial diabetes diagnosis is fasting blood sugar," Kautzky-Willer said.

Your fasting blood sugar is your blood sugar level when you haven't eaten for eight hours. It's just a single snapshot in time, however, and misses blood sugar spikes after a meal.

Fasting blood sugar "is generally lower in women than it is in men," Kautzky-Willer said. "It would make more sense to do a glucose tolerance test, but that is more work."

More complex tests for diabetes could save lives

A glucose tolerance test involves taking blood several times in the span of two hours, during which patients need to stay at the doctor's office.

Kautzky-Willer says it would be good if HbA1c levels were tested as well. Tests for HbA1c levels show a person's average blood sugar level over a two or three-month period.

HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin, which is when glucose in your body sticks to red blood cells. This prevents the body from using the sugar properly.

A high HbA1c means you have too much sugar in your blood and are more likely to develop diabetes complications. But testing HbA1c levels requires specialized lab equipment and is more expensive than testing the fasting blood sugar.

The glucose tolerance and the HbA1c tests are not covered by health insurance in Germany and Austria, only the fasting blood sugar one is covered, and that may be influencing the options for people in those countries.

Experts who spoke to DW agreed that to bring type 2 diabetes numbers down among young people, it's important to know when their blood values get close to the line for the disease, a condition known as being "pre-diabetic."

People who find out they have a problem at this early stage still have a chance to turn the ship around. With lifestyle and nutrition changes, diabetes progression can be stopped in some cases, saving them from a host of health problems later on, which may require regular medication and lead to a reduced life expectancy.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany
